how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Standby generator installation bid calculator

How much should I charge to install a standby generator?

Homeowners search that question and come back with one number. It hides everything that actually sets the price: the size of the machine, the length of the feeder, the transfer switch, and whether the fuel line is a short natural-gas tap or a far-yard propane run. A typical 22 kW natural-gas hang beside the house is not a far-yard propane set with a 400 A automatic transfer switch — and neither is what a flat "generator install" quote is pricing.

Open the free standby generator bid calculator

What a flat installed price cannot see

The feeder. Conductor size and run length between the generator and the transfer switch change with distance and amperage, not with a nameplate kW figure alone.

The transfer switch. An automatic transfer switch and a manual one are different equipment costs and different labor. Switch amperage — 100 A versus 400 A — changes both again.

The pad and setback. A precast pad and a poured pad are different costs, and clearance/setback requirements can add labor a "generator hang" line item never carries.

The fuel line. A short natural-gas tap and a far-yard propane run with its own tank placement are not the same trenching and piping job.

A bid you can defend

  1. Price the feeder and voltage-drop copper for the actual distance to the transfer switch.
  2. Price the transfer switch by type (automatic or manual) and amperage.
  3. Price the pad (precast or poured) and any setback labor.
  4. Price the fuel line for the actual run — natural gas or propane.
  5. Load the wage, then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin) for a walk-away number.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. The recommended-kW hint is a starting point, not a NEC 220 or manufacturer load calculation you can stamp or submit — confirm sizing and code compliance with a licensed electrician.

Worked example

A 22 kW natural-gas unit set on a precast pad beside the house, with a short feeder run to a 100 A automatic transfer switch and an existing gas line nearby, is a common, comparatively quick install. A far-yard placement for the same-size unit — driven by setback or noise requirements — with a longer feeder run, a 400 A ATS for a larger service, and a new propane tank and line, is a different job entirely, often several times the labor and material cost. The calculator prices both from the same inputs and reports dollars per kW so a homeowner's single "how much" number never has to guess which job theirs is.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a standby generator?

There is no flat installed price. A typical 22 kW natural-gas hang beside the house is a different job from a far-yard propane set with a 400 A automatic transfer switch. This calculator prices the feeder, the ATS, the pad, the fuel line, and the setback from your own wage and material inputs.

Is this a load calculation or a code ruling?

No. Outputs are arithmetic on the numbers you enter. The recommended-kW hint is a starting point, not a NEC 220 or manufacturer load calculation you can stamp or submit.

vs-a-flat-8000-generator-special.html.text:
← Standby Generator Installation Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $8,000 generator special

"$8,000 installed" is not a price for a standby-generator install — it is a price for one specific kW, fuel, service, and transfer switch, quietly applied to every house the truck pulls up to.

What a flat generator special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a search result, a postcard, or a Facebook ad, read off and repeated. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's ad will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one house — one kW, one fuel (usually natural gas), one service size, one transfer switch, beside the house, no trench — and then reused for every generator afterward, whether or not the next house looks anything like the one the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the generator size, load mode, fuel, service amps, transfer switch type and amps, pad type, location/setback, and gas meter, plus your loaded labor and overhead. It sizes the feeder from the nameplate current, prices the transfer switch that actually matches the service you entered, and returns a walk-away price for this house — not a generic one.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a 22 kW natural-gas hang beside the house or a 26 kW propane set in the far yard with a 60-foot trench and a 400 A ATS — a several-times difference in fuel line, trench, and switch cost for the same word "generator". Prices the feeder, fuel line, trench, and pad from the entered kW, fuel, and setback, so the two jobs above come out at $6,106.00 and $13,679.38 — about 2.2× — instead of one shared number.
Assumes the transfer switch on the truck matches the house, so a 400 A service quoted with a 200 A switch left over from the last job prices out at $6,607.83 with nothing to say the switch will not carry the whole house. Flags it directly: "The 200 A transfer switch is smaller than the 400 A service — it will not carry the whole house unless the load is split." Sizing the switch correctly for that same house prices at $9,685.14 — $3,077.31 more, and a switch that actually carries the load.
Sets a "target margin" by marking cost up a flat percentage — cost × 1.25 for a "25% margin" — which is a markup on cost, not a share of price. Solves for the price that makes margin exactly the stated share of that price. On the same $4,579.50 job, a 25% markup on cost prices at $5,724.37 and actually clears only 20.0% margin; this calculator's $6,106.00 clears the full 25% the target asked for.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the installer a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match the ad price. Reports the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus how many times a typical 22 kW natural-gas hang the entered house really is, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the installer commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one house it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat $8,000 generator special get the price wrong?

Because the feeder, the transfer switch, the fuel line, and the pad all scale with the generator's kW, the service amps, the fuel, and the setback, not with the word "generator" alone. A 22 kW natural-gas hang beside the house is a different job from a 26 kW propane set in the far yard with a 60-foot trench and a 400 A automatic transfer switch. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

Whether the transfer switch it assumes actually matches the service. A 400 A house still needs a 400 A automatic transfer switch, not the 200 A unit that happens to be on the truck or left over in a reused estimate. Swapping in the smaller, cheaper switch drops the price by real dollars and leaves a switch that will not carry the whole house on the panel.

Why does the transfer-switch warning matter if the dollar total looks fine?

Because the total by itself does not say which switch is behind it. A job priced with a correctly sized 400 A automatic transfer switch and the same job priced with an undersized 200 A one land at two different, both-plausible-looking totals — a flat number or a reused spreadsheet total gives no way to tell which total you are looking at. This calculator names the mismatch directly instead of leaving it to be read off a dollar figure that cannot carry that information.

What does solving margin as a share of price get right that a flat number misses?

A flat special, and most rough estimates built around one, price backward from a markup on cost — add 25% to what the job costs and call that the target margin. That is not the same number: margin is profit divided by price, not profit divided by cost, and a 25% markup on cost actually clears a lower margin than stated. This calculator solves for the price that hits the target margin exactly, so a target set at 25% comes out at 25%, not a smaller number wearing the same label.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, equipment cost, or what a competitor's postcard charges. It takes the generator size, load mode, fuel, service amps, transfer switch, pad, setback, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat number skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat generator special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running an electrical or generator-dealer company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one standby-generator install cost, given its machine, transfer switch, pad, and fuel line, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It serves HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and other trades with scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the electrical trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one job's generator size, load coverage (whole-house or essential circuits), fuel (natural gas or propane), service amps, transfer switch type and amps, pad type, location/setback, and gas meter, with feeder length, fuel-line length, and trench footage as their own line items, plus loaded crew wage, payroll burden, permit fee, generator hardware and other materials, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the installed price, dollars per kW, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
